Bridges add no new facts; any fact carries card cites (checked chapter citations). See work/drafts/pathway-anchor-requests.md for anchors the site must add.

pathways.title: A First Reading
pathways.intro: The shortest route through the whole story, from a pipeline merger to a new federal law. You will read parts of five chapters and meet three people from the Cast of Characters. Use the arrows in the pathway bar, and read each stop at your own pace.

stops.label: Chapter 1: Growing fast
stops.bridge: Start with the numbers Enron reported as it grew. As you read, keep two measures apart: revenue (how much a company sells) and profit (what it keeps).

stops.label: Chapter 2: What mark-to-market accounting means
stops.bridge: This is the accounting method at the heart of the story. Work through the made-up example and its diagram, and notice that the cash is the same either way; only the timing of the reported profit changes.

stops.label: Chapter 3: What a special purpose entity is
stops.bridge: Read the opening and the first diagram, then move on. The key question is the 3% test: was an independent owner's own money really at risk?

stops.label: Chapter 3: What it added up to
stops.bridge: Skip ahead to the chapter's summary. Notice what the investigators said about how clearly Enron's public filings described these deals.

stops.label: Cast: Andrew Fastow
stops.bridge: The board approved Fastow, Enron's chief financial officer, as the general partner of the LJM partnerships you just read about. Read his outcome closely: the Cast uses exact legal words such as alleged, pleaded guilty, and sentenced.

cites.loc: pp. 68-70, III.A Formation and Authorization of LJM Cayman, L.P. and LJM2, lines 2625-2674
pp. 70-73, III.A Formation and Authorization of LJM Cayman, L.P. and LJM2, lines 2694-2775

stops.label: Chapter 5: November 8, the restatement
stops.bridge: Here Enron told investors not to rely on four years of its audited financial statements. As you read, connect the corrections to the entities from Chapter 3.

cites.loc: p. 1, Press release, Nov 8, 2001 (Exhibit 99.1), lines 44-47

stops.label: Chapter 5: November 28 to December 2
stops.bridge: Notice how quickly the end came once confidence was gone, and notice where the sources disagree about why the rescue merger failed.

stops.label: Cast: Kenneth Lay
stops.bridge: Read Lay's outcome slowly, word by word. What does it mean, in law, that a conviction was vacated?

stops.label: Cast: Jeffrey Skilling
stops.bridge: Compare what the jury decided with what the appeals courts did afterwards. Which parts of the outcome does the library leave open?

stops.label: Chapter 7: A new law
stops.bridge: Finish with Congress's response. For each change in the list, try to name the problem from an earlier stop that it was meant to address.

pathways.closing_question: Enron's numbers were checked by its own managers, its board, its auditor, and outside analysts. Which of those checks do you think failed first, and why?

pathways.title: Mark-to-Market Explained
pathways.intro: Mark-to-market accounting values a contract or an investment at its current market value, and counts any change in that value as profit or loss right away. This pathway explains the idea in plain language, then follows it through Enron's trading contracts, its investments, and the structures built to protect its gains on paper.

stops.label: Glossary: mark-to-market accounting
stops.bridge: Begin with the short definition. Two related ideas, fair value and unrealized gain, come up at every later stop.

stops.label: Glossary: unrealized gain
stops.bridge: An unrealized gain is a profit on paper: the value has gone up, but nothing has been sold and no cash has arrived. Keep this idea in mind for the rest of the pathway.

stops.label: Timeline: mark-to-market accounting for trading
stops.bridge: Enron began using the method early. Notice that the sources give two different starting years, 1991 and 1992, and that the site reports both instead of choosing one.

cites.loc: p. 62, Part Two, II.B.2, footnote 67
p. 32, Part One II (SEC's mark-to-market determination)

stops.label: Chapter 2: What mark-to-market accounting means
stops.bridge: Work through the ten-year contract example with the diagram. When a contract has no market price, ask who produces the estimate of what it is worth.

stops.label: Chapter 2: Marking investments to market
stops.bridge: Here the same idea is applied to Enron's stakes in other companies. Notice how the stock price of a company Enron had invested in could move Enron's own reported profit.

stops.label: Chapter 3: Rhythms, a hedge with Enron's own stock (Follow the Money lens)
stops.bridge: Mark-to-market now creates a problem: a paper gain that could disappear if the stock fell. Read how Enron tried to protect that gain, and why the board's special committee found that this was not a normal hedge.

cites.loc: p. 13 (also pp. 82-83), Executive Summary - Hedging Transactions; IV.C.1, lines 698-712, 3054-3066

stops.label: Chapter 3: The Raptor diagram
stops.bridge: The Raptors extended the same approach to many investments. Trace in the diagram where the money to cover a loss would have come from.

stops.label: Chapter 5: The restatement chart
stops.bridge: Profits that rest on estimates and on accounting choices can later be corrected. Compare the reported and restated profit for each year, then read the section to see which corrections the restatement involved.

stops.label: Chapter 2: Ask Why
stops.bridge: Return to the question at the end of Chapter 2, now that you have seen the method at work.

pathways.closing_question: Mark-to-market accounting can give investors more up-to-date information, but it depends on estimates. What safeguards would make you trust a company's own estimate of what a long-term contract is worth?

pathways.title: The Special Purpose Entities
pathways.intro: Special purpose entities were at the center of Enron's accounting. This pathway follows how they worked, from the basic rule to Chewco, the LJM partnerships and the Raptors. It then shows how Enron described these deals in its annual report, and what happened to two of the people who ran them.

stops.label: Chapter 3: What an SPE is, and the 3% test
stops.bridge: Read the opening and the first diagram carefully. Everything that follows turns on one question: was an independent owner's own money truly at risk?

stops.label: Glossary: the 3% rule
stops.bridge: A quick look at the rule itself before you see it tested.

stops.label: Chapter 3: Chewco (Follow the Money lens)
stops.bridge: With Follow the Money on, track where Chewco's equity came from, and what the board's special committee concluded that meant for the 3% test.

stops.label: Chapter 3: The Chewco and LJM diagram
stops.bridge: Use the diagram to see who sat on each side of these deals.

stops.label: Chapter 3: The LJM partnerships (The Board lens)
stops.bridge: With The Board on, notice what the board approved and which controls it relied on: two senior officers were to approve every LJM2 deal, and the Audit Committee was to review them each year.

cites.loc: pp. 70-73, III.A Formation and Authorization of LJM Cayman, L.P. and LJM2, lines 2694-2775

stops.label: Chapter 3: The Raptors (Follow the Money lens)
stops.bridge: Notice where the Raptors' ability to pay came from, and what happened when Enron's stock and the investments they covered fell at the same time.

stops.label: The Footnote: "a senior officer of Enron"
stops.bridge: Now read how Enron's annual report described these deals. This annotation looks at how the note referred to the person who ran the partnerships.

stops.label: The Footnote: "to hedge certain merchant investments"
stops.bridge: The note calls these deals hedges. Compare its wording with what you read about the Raptors two stops ago.

stops.label: Cast: Andrew Fastow
stops.bridge: Read how Fastow's cases ended, and notice where two government announcements give different figures.

stops.label: Cast: Michael Kopper
stops.bridge: Kopper, who worked for Fastow, took Fastow's place at Chewco. Read what the library shows about his case, and what it does not show.

cites.loc: pp. 43-44, II.A Formation of Chewco, lines 1702-1727

pathways.closing_question: An SPE could stay off Enron's books if an independent owner had at least 3% of its value at risk. Why might a rule based on a single number be easier to get around than a rule based on who really bears the risk?

pathways.title: Andersen's Fall and the Big Five to Big Four
pathways.intro: This pathway follows Enron's auditor, Arthur Andersen: the audit and its fees, the warning signs, the destruction of documents, the firm's criminal case and what the Supreme Court decided, and how the audit profession changed afterwards.

stops.label: Chapter 6: Why auditors matter (The Auditors lens)
stops.bridge: Read the opening and "Enron's auditor." Notice who pays the auditor, and why that makes independence so important.

stops.label: Chapter 4: "Many push limits" (The Auditors lens)
stops.bridge: Here is the Andersen lead partner's own handwritten note about Enron's accounting, as the Senate subcommittee staff reported it. Compare it with what the Audit Committee's chair testified he recalled hearing.

cites.loc: p. 17, Factual Basis for Findings (High Risk Accounting)

stops.label: Chapter 6: The fees
stops.bridge: Notice that the sources give different fee totals, and that Andersen disputed calling some of the work consulting. Why would that label matter?

stops.label: Cast: Joseph Berardino
stops.bridge: Andersen's chief executive. Before reading his entry, look back at "Errors and what the examiner concluded" in Chapter 6. Then read what the library records about him, and what it does not show.

cites.loc: pp. 113, 115-116, Appendix: 'Remarks of Joseph F. Berardino, Managing Partner - Chief Executive Officer, Andersen' (prepared statement) (PDF pages covered: 119, 121-122)

stops.label: Chapter 6: The shredding
stops.bridge: The witnesses did not all agree about what happened. As you read, keep track of who said what, and in what setting.

stops.label: Cast: David Duncan
stops.bridge: Andersen's lead partner on Enron. Read his outcome carefully, including what the library does not yet show.

cites.loc: p. 2, Complaint, para. 5 (Defendant)

stops.label: Cast: Nancy Temple
stops.bridge: The Andersen lawyer whose e-mail about the document policy is quoted in Chapter 6. Notice what the Cast says about charges.

cites.loc: p. 45, Hearing record exhibit (e-mail dated 10/12/2001 from Nancy A. Temple to Michael C. Odom)

stops.label: Chapter 6: Conviction, collapse, reversal
stops.bridge: The Supreme Court reversed Andersen's conviction in 2005. Read exactly why, and what the reversal did and did not decide. The numbered notes link to the Court's opinion in the source library.

cites.loc: p. 544 U.S. at 697, Reporter's line preceding the opinion

stops.label: Timeline: auditor events
stops.bridge: The timeline is filtered to auditor events. Scroll through them to see the whole relationship, from the 1985 merger to the 2005 decision.

stops.label: Chapter 6: The Big Four
stops.bridge: Finish with the effect on the profession. Notice what the GAO said it had found, and what it said it had not yet found.

pathways.closing_question: An auditor is paid by the company it checks. After reading Andersen's story, what arrangements would you want in place so that an auditor can say no to its most important client?

pathways.title: From Enron to Sarbanes-Oxley and the PCAOB
pathways.intro: This pathway starts with Chapter 7's list of what the Sarbanes-Oxley Act changed. It then goes provision by provision through "Why This Matters to You," linking each rule to the Enron problem it addressed, and ends with what these rules mean for someone starting a career.

stops.label: Chapter 7: A new law
stops.bridge: Read the list of the law's main changes. The next stops take several of them in more detail.

stops.label: Timeline: the law is signed
stops.bridge: Place the law in time. Use the year links to look back at how close it came to the events of 2001 and early 2002.

stops.label: Why This Matters: CEO and CFO certification
stops.bridge: The chief executive and chief financial officer must now personally certify each annual and quarterly report. Think back to the executives in the Cast of Characters as you read.

cites.loc: Sec. 302(a)

stops.label: Why This Matters: internal control reporting
stops.bridge: Internal controls are a company's own checks on its numbers. Recall the controls the board placed around the LJM2 deals in Chapter 3.

cites.loc: pp. 70-73, III.A Formation and Authorization of LJM Cayman, L.P. and LJM2, lines 2694-2775

stops.label: Why This Matters: the PCAOB
stops.bridge: Read what the new oversight board does. Compare it with Chapter 6's account of Andersen.

stops.label: Timeline: the PCAOB is ready
stops.bridge: Notice how much time passed between the law's signing and the day the new overseer was ready to operate.

stops.label: Why This Matters: auditor independence
stops.bridge: Chapter 6 described Andersen's fees for audit work and for other work. Read which services the law now limits, and why.

stops.label: Why This Matters: document destruction and whistleblowers
stops.bridge: Two earlier stories meet here: the shredding at Andersen, and the letter Sherron Watkins testified she sent to Lay. Ask how each might have gone differently under the new rules.

cites.loc: p. 32, Testimony of C.E. Andrews, Andersen (oral)
p. 12, Statement of Sherron Watkins

stops.label: Why This Matters: what it means for you
stops.bridge: Finish with the part written for you. Notice where the page says the library's documents stop.

pathways.closing_question: If you could add one more rule based on the Enron story, what would it be, and which stop on this pathway supports your choice?

pathways.title: Reading the Footnotes
pathways.for_whom: Anyone learning to read an annual report
pathways.intro: The notes at the back of an annual report explain the numbers in front. The famous Note 16 was only one piece of the story: other notes in Enron's 2000 annual report held other pieces, and later filings and investigations showed what they left out. This pathway reads several notes together, then compares them with what came later.

stops.label: Glossary: notes to the financial statements
stops.bridge: Start with what notes are for. As you go, ask of each note two questions: what could a careful reader learn here, and what could no reader learn?

stops.label: Note 1: accounting policies
stops.bridge: Note 1 said Enron's statements included "all subsidiaries controlled by Enron Corp." Keep the word "controlled" in mind: whether Enron had to consolidate an entity depended on rules about who controlled it and who bore its risk.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 1 Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, lines 4091-4099

stops.label: Note 3: the trading book
stops.bridge: Note 3 reported about $21.5 billion of trading assets at fair value, and cautioned that the face amounts of its contracts did not measure its real exposure to risk. Ask how a reader could tell how much of that value came from Enron's own estimates.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 3 Price Risk Management Activities, Fair Value, lines 4431-4452
Form 10-K 2000, Note 3, Notional Amounts and Terms, lines 4415-4421

stops.label: Note 4: merchant investments
stops.bridge: Note 4 said these investments were valued using market prices, independent appraisals and cash flow analyses. Compare it with what Chapter 3 says about the Raptors, which were set up to offset losses on the same kind of investment.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 4 Merchant Activities, lines 4634-4674
p. 97, V. The Raptors (introduction), lines 3592-3612

stops.label: Note 9: affiliates kept off the books
stops.bridge: Note 9 listed JEDI and Whitewing, each 50% owned and not consolidated. The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee staff later reported that experts pointed to this pattern, just below the level that requires consolidation, as a reason to look closer.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 9 Unconsolidated Equity Affiliates (tables), lines 5014-5078
p. 29, SEC's review of Enron's filings

stops.label: Note 16: related party transactions
stops.bridge: Now read the famous note phrase by phrase. Note 9 had already mentioned "the Related Party" and pointed ahead to this note; here is what that label covered.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 9 Unconsolidated Equity Affiliates, lines 5122-5140

stops.label: Note 15: commitments and guarantees
stops.bridge: Note 15 listed Enron's guarantees and said management did not consider it likely that Enron would have to pay. Ask what a reader would need to know to judge that for themselves.

cites.loc: Form 10-K 2000, Note 15 Commitments, lines 5811-5856

stops.label: The third-quarter 2001 report
stops.bridge: In November 2001, Enron's quarterly report named the Raptors and set out their terms. The Senate subcommittee staff contrasted its nine-page account with the one-page notes of earlier years.

cites.loc: pp. 22-23, Note 4 Related Party Transactions - Portfolio SPEs, lines 1543-1563
p. 48, Finding (4) - Inadequate Public Disclosure

stops.label: Chapter 5: November 8, the restatement
stops.bridge: Here Enron itself said that three entities should have been consolidated, and that its financial statements for 1997 through 2000 should not be relied upon. Compare that with the wording of Note 1.

cites.loc: pp. 1, 4-5, Item 5; 2.A Restatement Number 1, lines 51-72, 263-284
p. 1, Press release, Nov 8, 2001 (Exhibit 99.1), lines 44-47

stops.label: Chapter 4: The watchdogs outside
stops.bridge: Finally, who was supposed to read these notes closely? The Senate staff report said that if the SEC had reviewed Enron's 2000 annual report, items such as Note 16 were likely to have prompted questions.

cites.loc: p. 28, Part One II (SEC review of Enron filings)

pathways.closing_question: Enron's notes disclosed many facts, yet investigators later found that readers could not see what was going on. Is a disclosure honest if it is accurate but impossible to understand? Who should decide whether a note is clear enough?

handout.closing_question: Enron's notes disclosed many facts, yet investigators later found that readers could not see what was going on. Is a disclosure honest if it is accurate but impossible to understand? Who should decide whether a note is clear enough?
discussion_questions: Pick one note from this pathway. List one thing a careful reader could learn from it, and one thing the reader could not learn.
Several notes pointed to each other (Note 9 to Note 16, for example). Does spreading information across notes help or hinder a reader?
Compare the one-page Note 16 with the nine-page account in the November 2001 quarterly report. Why might Enron have written more clearly the second time?
